input: The separation of ethanol from water by binary distillation is a well-established operation, and the Fenske equation provides a widely used shortcut method for estimating the minimum number of theoretical stages required for a specified separation. In this case, the relative volatility of the mixture is taken as 1.5, and it is assumed to remain constant throughout the column, which greatly simplifies the calculation. The product specifications are demanding: the distillate is required to contain 98 mol% of the light component, while the bottoms stream may contain no more than 2 mol% of the light component. Applying the Fenske equation to these specifications yields a minimum stage count of 19.2 theoretical stages, a figure that includes the reboiler. It is important to note that this value represents an idealised lower bound that corresponds to total reflux, and it cannot be achieved in a real, operating column. In practice, the actual design operates at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio, and the number of stages required at that reflux ratio cannot be obtained from the Fenske equation alone; instead, it is determined by means of a separate, more rigorous simulation. Overall, the Fenske result of 19.2 stages provides a useful benchmark against which the simulation result can be compared, ensuring that the final design is grounded in a sound theoretical minimum.
target: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 1.5, taken as constant over the column. Specifications are 98 mol% light component in the distillate and 2 mol% light component in the bottoms. For these specifications the Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 19.2 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The minimum stage count is the stage count at total reflux. It is a lower bound on any operating design, not a design value: a column at finite reflux needs more stages than the minimum, by an amount the Fenske equation does not fix. The constant relative volatility is part of the result as stated. A column in which the volatility changes appreciably from stage to stage is not described by the count, and the count is not transferred to such a column without a stage-by-stage calculation. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. The stage count at the design reflux therefore comes from a separate simulation at that reflux, not from the Fenske result. The simulation result is read against the floor of 19.2 stages. A simulated count below the floor would show an error in the simulation; the margin above the floor is the stage cost of running at finite reflux rather than at total reflux. The minimum also sets the terms on which the reflux choice is judged: a reflux ratio below the minimum has no stage count at any column height, so the operating point must stand above the minimum reflux before the stage question arises at all.
